Read it column by column. The empirical risk falls fast and then crawls; it even goes up between 80 and 100 rounds, the same wobble as on the ten messages. The bound ZTZ_TZT​ sits above it every time, and falls every time, as the proof promised. The gap climbs steadily. The certified risk, their sum, falls to about 0.175 near 40 rounds and climbs again. In this run, any TTT from 23 to 64 certifies a true risk of at most 0.20.

And the fresh error? It keeps falling all the way to 80 rounds. The certificate holds for every distribution and every vote in the class, so it charges you for the class’s size even when, as here, the extra rounds happen not to hurt. It is what you can promise in writing, not a prediction.

Fix the bug

Back to the inbox. Your manager wants the filter shipped with a written promise: with probability at least 95%, its true risk on fresh mail is at most 0.20. You have the twenty thousand labelled messages and the stump learner. The only dial is the number of rounds.

In the lab you set TTT, from 1 to 100, and train. You see the empirical risk, the bound ZTZ_TZT​ falling under it, the gap growing, and the certified risk. Too few rounds, and the vote can’t express the true labelling: the empirical risk alone is above 0.20. Too many, and the class is so large that the gap alone eats your margin. Find a TTT whose certified risk is at most 0.20, and ship.

[lab-act2: built on the lesson page]

What people get wrong

“AdaBoost’s empirical risk goes down every round.” It doesn’t have to. On the ten messages it stayed at 0.2 after round 2, and on the twenty thousand it went up between rounds 80 and 100. What goes down every round is ZtZ_tZt​, the average of e−yift(xi)e^{-y_i f_t(x_i)}e−yi​ft​(xi​), which sits above the empirical risk.

“More rounds means a better filter.” More rounds means a lower empirical risk and a bigger class, whose VC dimension grows roughly linearly with TTT. In the lab’s run, 100 rounds have a smaller empirical risk than 40, and a certified risk of 0.227 instead of 0.175.

“A weak learner is a bad learner, so boosting is a trick.” The weak learner promises an edge of γ\gammaγ on every distribution over the examples, not just the uniform one: a strong assumption in disguise, and exactly what the proof uses each round. A stump that is right 63% of the time on the original mail but can’t beat a coin once the weights move gives AdaBoost nothing to work with.

“The theorem says AdaBoost learns.” The theorem is about the empirical risk only. It says nothing about fresh mail. That part needs the size of L(B,T)L(B, T)L(B,T), and the two together make the tradeoff you just navigated.

Faces: boosting in the wild

The same recipe, counts plus stumps plus boosting, made one of the best-known detectors in computer vision: the face detector of Viola and Jones. The task is to tell whether a small grey image, 24 by 24 pixels, shows a human face. So X\mathcal XX is the set of 24×2424 \times 2424×24 real matrices of grey levels, and the goal is a hypothesis h:X→{±1}h: \mathcal X \to \{\pm 1\}h:X→{±1}.

Each base hypothesis has the form h(x)=f(g(x))h(x) = f(g(x))h(x)=f(g(x)), where fff is a decision stump on a single number and ggg turns the image into that number. Every ggg is described by two things:

  • an axis-aligned rectangle RRR inside the image, and
  • a type, one of four masks, A to D.

To compute ggg, stretch the mask to fill RRR, add up the pixel values in each of the mask’s regions, and take a difference. Types A and B split the rectangle into two equal halves, side by side or one above the other, and subtract one sum from the other. Type C splits it into three strips and subtracts the two outer sums from the centre one. Type D splits it into four quarters and takes the difference between the diagonal pairs.

[diagram:haar: built on the lesson page]

How many functions ggg are there? A rectangle is fixed by its two horizontal and two vertical edges, so there are at most 24424^4244 rectangles and 4⋅2444 \cdot 24^44⋅244 functions. Counting more carefully, the edges sit on 25 grid lines in each direction:

rectangles = (25 * 24 // 2) ** 2
print(rectangles, 24 ** 4, 4 * rectangles)

It prints 90000 331776 360000. So the weak learner is the stump learner of this lesson, run over a few hundred thousand features: compute every ggg on every training image once, then find the best stump on the weighted images in each round. The first step is made fast by a preprocessing trick, the integral image, which lets every rectangle sum be computed in constant time. Problem 3 asks you to invent it.

And what does AdaBoost pick? The first feature it chooses compares the band across the eyes with the band across the upper cheeks just below: the eye region is often darker than the cheeks. The second compares the eye regions with the bridge of the nose between them. Nobody told the learner that faces have eyes. It found the two cheapest rules of thumb that beat a coin, then the next one, on the faces the first two missed.

Where boosting came from

Boosting began as a purely theoretical question. In 1988 Kearns and Valiant asked whether an efficient weak learner can always be “boosted” into an efficient strong learner. Robert Schapire, then a graduate student at MIT, answered yes in 1990, but his construction was not practical. In 1995 Freund and Schapire proposed AdaBoost, the first truly practical boosting algorithm, and it became hugely popular: a rare case of a question asked for its own sake turning into a tool everyone uses.

The question also runs in reverse. If strong learning of a class is computationally hard, then so is weak learning of it, since a weak learner could be boosted. That makes boosting useful for proving hardness results, too.

Recap and the next bug

  1. A decision stump compares one feature with a threshold. ERM over stumps, for any distribution over the examples, runs in O(dm)O(dm)O(dm) time per call after sorting each feature once, using the update F←F+yiDiF \leftarrow F + y_i D_iF←F+yi​Di​.
  2. A γ\gammaγ-weak learner only promises true risk at most 12−γ\tfrac12 - \gamma21​−γ. Statistically that is no easier than strong learning (infinite VC dimension rules out both), but it can be much easier computationally.
  3. AdaBoost reweights the examples each round so that the last hypothesis’s mistakes carry more weight, and gives each hypothesis the vote wt=12log⁡(1/εt−1)w_t = \tfrac12\log(1/\varepsilon_t - 1)wt​=21​log(1/εt​−1), the vote that shrinks ZtZ_tZt​ the most.
  4. If every round has an edge of γ\gammaγ, the empirical risk after TTT rounds is at most e−2γ2Te^{-2\gamma^2 T}e−2γ2T. The proof bounds the empirical risk by ZTZ_TZT​, splits ZTZ_TZT​ into a product of per-round ratios, and computes each ratio exactly as 2εt(1−εt)2\sqrt{\varepsilon_t(1 - \varepsilon_t)}2εt​(1−εt​)​.
  5. AdaBoost returns a member of L(B,T)L(B, T)L(B,T), a halfspace on top of TTT base hypotheses. Its VC dimension is at least TTT for stumps on the line, and at most about TTT times the base class’s, up to a logarithm. The number of rounds is a dial for the tradeoff between approximation and estimation error.

Your filter ships with its promise, and the inbox is quiet. Then the questions start. Why stumps, and not small trees two levels deep? Why these ten words, and not fifty? Why 40 rounds? The certificate you used covered your choice of TTT, because you paid for all hundred values up front. But for every other knob you turned, you looked at the same twenty thousand labels, tried several settings, and kept whichever looked best on them. Each choice tuned on the same labels makes those labels look better than fresh mail will. Pay for every knob up front, and the certificate becomes too loose to say anything. So how do you choose the rounds, the depth and the features without fooling yourself? That is the next lesson: model selection and validation.
